title: Solite Corp. v. EPA
lead: EPA narrowed a temporary mineral-waste exemption, and industry challenges required the court to distinguish permissible technical supplementation from a decisive new methodology disclosed too late.

actors.name: Environmental Protection Agency
actors.role: Agency defining mineral-processing wastes temporarily exempt under Bevill

actors.name: Companies, trade associations, and Baltimore
actors.role: Petitioners challenging general criteria and particular streams

actors.name: Solite and Du Pont
actors.role: Petitioners obtaining relief on specified waste determinations

proceedings: EPA issued September 1989 and January 1990 rules retaining twenty processing wastes.
D.C. Circuit largely upheld the rules, vacated lightweight aggregate determination, and remanded specified other matters.
Court denied EPA rehearing on mixtures and permits February 26, 1992.
limits: The court applied then-governing Chevron review. Loss of Bevill status alone did not establish Subtitle C hazardous-waste regulation. Remands on Du Pont, mixtures, and permits did not themselves award exemptions or decide all merits.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress pauses regulation while requiring study
sections.cue: Earlier litigation narrows EPA’s initial interpretation
paragraphs: The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, established a comprehensive hazardous-waste system in Subtitle C. The Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA, proposed a special category for high-volume, relatively low-hazard wastes in 1978 but abandoned it in May 1980. Congress then enacted the Bevill Amendment, temporarily withholding Subtitle C regulation for extraction, beneficiation, and processing of ores and minerals while requiring a study, report, and regulatory determination.

EPA initially read the exemption broadly and provisionally across exploration, mining, milling, smelting, and refining. It missed the study deadline. Litigation produced distinct schedules for extraction/beneficiation and processing, and the circuit’s EDF II decision rejected continued overbroad processing coverage. EPA had to identify the high-volume, low-hazard special wastes Congress intended.

sections.title: Successive proposals set volume and hazard screens
sections.cue: Industry challenges both the criteria and particular classifications
paragraphs: An October 1988 proposal used 50,000 metric tons annually per facility. April 1989 separated solids and liquids, retained that solids figure, proposed 1.5 million tons for liquids, and added low-hazard screening. The September final rule used newer survey data and set 45,000 tons for solids and one million for liquids, with toxicity/mobility and corrosivity screens. Another proposal and January 1990 rule completed twenty retained processing wastes.

Companies, trade associations, and Baltimore challenged authority, notice and access to data, methods, and individual streams. Denying Bevill status did not alone put a waste under Subtitle C; it also needed a relevant hazardous characteristic. Under the Chevron framework then governing, imprecise statutory concepts left room for reasonable standards consistent with EDF II, while technical explanations received arbitrary-and-capricious review.

sections.title: Most general criteria survive
sections.cue: Confirming new data differs from a newly devised method
paragraphs: The unanimous panel distinguished screening into the exempt category from the later comprehensive study of wastes within it. Congress did not require the same multifactor study twice. EPA reasonably used volumes already managed under Subtitle C to assess technical feasibility.

Meaningful Administrative Procedure Act § 553 notice required access to supporting technical material. Yet supplementary data confirming a method or correcting deficiencies need not always reopen comments absent prejudice. EPA’s newer treatment, storage, disposal, and recycling survey replaced the older Biennial Report without substantially changing the threshold methodology. Petitioners identified neither inaccurate replacement data nor concealment; the added data answered industry criticisms and confirmed the analysis.

The agency adequately justified land-disposal and wastewater facilities, commercial facilities, largest streams, separate solid/liquid thresholds, and a 95th-percentile cutoff allowing 5% overlap. A troubling dispute over partially aggregated data did not overcome its conscientious disaggregation and reasonable stream-specific approach.

Volume was not the only permissible screen. Regulatory history and EDF II included low hazard; EDF I’s treatment of extraction and beneficiation did not forbid processing-entry screening. EPA explained its developing Method 1312 leaching test and relaxed corrosivity range and cross-checked results without needing scientific certainty. A separate liquid-test issue was unnecessary because both affected wastes failed independently.

sections.title: Other general challenges fail but the mixture premise disappears
sections.cue: Derivative rules return to the agency
paragraphs: EPA reasonably limited feedstocks to less than 50% scrap, including designated in-process materials, distinguishing primary from secondary processing despite recycling concerns. A one-time designation rather than continual expansion to future streams was permissible. EPA could likewise interpret the Simpson Amendment’s relaxed-control authority as concerning the same special-waste category; legislative materials did not compel broader coverage.

EPA also applied the Subtitle C mixture rule to Bevill/non-Bevill combinations and required treatment permits for mixing. The separate Shell Oil decision had vacated the underlying mixture rule procedurally. This court remanded the derivative Bevill rule and permit requirement without deciding their substantive validity. EPA could adopt a valid underlying rule or supply an independent justification; the court did not decree every mixture exempt or all permits forbidden.

sections.title: Du Pont’s classification lacks an explanation
paragraphs: Du Pont’s chloride-ilmenite process generated iron chloride gas during initial beneficiation and titanium tetrachloride during subsequent processing in the same vessel. The iron chloride later condensed into acid waste. EPA classified it as processing waste based on physical inseparability and similarity to conventional chloride operations, without explaining why coexistence outweighed the temporal distinction or why the similarities controlled. The court required explanation or reconsideration, not automatic coverage. SCM had not presented its comparable argument to the agency, and its process was not obviously identical, so it received no parallel relief.

For chrome tailings, EPA could distinguish treated low-hazard material from untreated landfill residue lacking a low-hazard showing. Recognition of treated material after comments required no fresh round simply because other arguments failed, and possible future regeneration did not satisfy the sustained one-time volume inquiry. For lead wastewater, measuring separate streams as generated rather than combining them as managed was reasonable, as was the low-hazard analysis using two of five plants.

sections.title: Lightweight aggregate crosses the line into a new undisclosed method
sections.cue: The final result is principally affirmance with defined exceptions
paragraphs: EPA initially estimated lightweight-aggregate air-pollution-control dust/sludge at 134,000 tons annually per facility, above the solids threshold, and proposed retention. Audubon questioned usable answers from only six of twenty-eight facilities. EPA then turned to different survey questions and new inferential calculations, reducing the estimate to 15,813 tons. Solite received an explanatory memorandum January 11, 1990, only one day before the Administrator signed the rule.

Unlike the general survey substitution, this changed both methodology and relevant data without meaningful comment. The proposal had not signaled reconsideration of that volume determination. One informal day was insufficient, and parties need not monitor everyone else’s comments to discover changes the agency should disclose. The court required notice and comment without deciding whether the lower estimate was substantively correct.

On December 31, 1991, Judges Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Douglas H. Ginsburg, and Randolph issued the per curiam decision. Most rules survived; the lightweight determination was vacated, Du Pont’s classification remanded for explanation or reconsideration, and mixtures and permits remanded without merits resolution. On February 26, 1992, the court denied EPA rehearing on the last two matters because its proposed Shell Oil distinction had not been briefed originally, while leaving appropriate distinctions open on remand.
